WAF, OWASP, SAST and DAST: How do these: OWASP guidance defines common application risks and secure practices; SAST examines source or compiled code before deployment; DAST probes a running application; and a WAF mitigates selected malicious request patterns at runtime. Use all four as complementary layers, validate findings, tune false positives, and never treat WAF rules as a substitute for fixing vulnerable code.
WAF and OWASP scenario: A new managed WA: Move or return the rule to preview/log-only mode, identify the exact OWASP rule signature and request element causing the match, and confirm no real attack is hidden in the traffic. Add the narrowest exclusion, test representative malicious and legitimate payloads, redeploy progressively, monitor false positives, and keep the application-level vulnerability remediation separate.
SAST and DAST pipeline design: Where sho: Run fast SAST and dependency/secret scans during pull requests, then authenticated DAST against an isolated deployed environment. Gate releases on validated critical/high findings based on exploitability and policy, with documented time-bound exceptions; retain evidence and route findings to owners rather than failing builds on untriaged noise.
MongoDB and Redis: When would you use ea: Use MongoDB as a durable document database when flexible document models and query/index capabilities fit the domain; use Redis for low-latency cache, session, counters, rate limits, or ephemeral coordination. Keep the durable source of truth clear, define cache invalidation and TTLs, protect both with authentication/TLS/network controls, and avoid using Redis as durable storage unless its persistence/HA trade-offs are explicitly accepted.
MongoDB and Redis failure scenario: Redi: Fail open or degrade for non-critical cache use by reading MongoDB directly with rate protection, but fail safely for functions where Redis provides correctness such as distributed locks. Use timeouts, circuit breakers, bounded retries, cache stampede protection, and monitoring; restore Redis gradually and warm only important keys rather than flooding MongoDB.
MongoDB and Redis performance: How would: Use traces to separate MongoDB query time from Redis lookup/network time, then inspect cache hit rate, evictions, memory fragmentation, slow logs, connection pools, Mongo indexes and query plans, replication lag, and saturation. Fix the actual layer—index/query, cache key/TTL, pool, or capacity—and validate p95/p99 latency and error rates afterward.
Data structures and algorithms: How do y: Start from required operations and constraints: lookup, insertion, ordering, range queries, traversal, memory, concurrency, and expected data size. Compare complexity and real constants—for example hash maps for average O(1) lookup, heaps for priority selection, trees for ordered operations, and graphs for relationships—then validate with representative inputs rather than choosing from habit.
Data structures and algorithms coding qu: Maintain a hash map of key frequencies, then use a min-heap of size K to keep the highest-frequency entries, producing O(n log k) time and O(m + k) space for m distinct keys. For an unbounded distributed stream, use windowing and approximate structures such as Count-Min Sketch when exact global counts are too expensive.
Data structures and algorithms scenario:: Use depth-first search with three states—unvisited, visiting, and visited; an edge to a visiting node is a back edge and proves a cycle. Complexity is O(V+E). Kahn's topological-sort algorithm is an alternative: if fewer than V vertices can be removed through zero-indegree processing, a cycle exists.
ELK, OpenTelemetry and Jaeger: How would: Use OpenTelemetry SDKs/collectors to generate and route standardized traces, metrics, and optionally logs; store/search logs in Elasticsearch and visualize them through Kibana; send traces to Jaeger or another compatible backend. Propagate trace IDs into structured logs so engineers can move from a latency trace to the relevant ELK records, while controlling sampling, retention, and cardinality.
ELK and OpenTelemetry incident: Logs are: Verify trace context propagation across every service and inject trace_id/span_id into structured log fields through the OpenTelemetry logging integration or application logger. Normalize field names in Logstash/index templates, confirm sampling retained the trace, and add a Kibana link/query using the trace ID; parsing a trace ID from message text is a fragile fallback.
OpenTelemetry and Jaeger scaling: How wo: Use head sampling for baseline control and tail sampling in the collector to retain errors, slow traces, and important routes, while dropping noisy health checks. Apply attribute allow-lists, prevent high-cardinality resource labels, batch/compress exports, scale collectors, and set tiered Elasticsearch/trace retention based on operational value.
PostgreSQL and MySQL: What factors would: Both are mature relational databases, so choose using required SQL features, extensions, JSON/geospatial needs, replication/HA model, operational expertise, managed-cloud support, licensing/ecosystem, and migration constraints. PostgreSQL is often favored for advanced SQL and extensibility, while MySQL has a broad web ecosystem; benchmark the actual workload instead of relying on generic rankings.
PostgreSQL and MySQL migration: How woul: Inventory schema, data types, indexes, procedures, isolation behavior, and application SQL differences; create and validate the target schema, perform bulk load, then use CDC to replicate changes. Run consistency checks and shadow/read tests, rehearse cutover and rollback, freeze or redirect writes briefly, and monitor correctness and performance after switching.
PostgreSQL and MySQL troubleshooting: A: Inspect slow-query logs and execution plans, lock waits/deadlocks, connection-pool saturation, CPU/IO/cache hit rate, replication lag, transaction duration, and application traces. Optimize queries/indexes and transaction scope first, then adjust pooling or capacity; adding connections can make an overloaded database worse.
Event-driven architecture: What are the: Events decouple producers and consumers, absorb bursts, enable asynchronous workflows, and allow independent scaling, but introduce eventual consistency, duplicate/out-of-order delivery, schema evolution, observability, and operational complexity. Use it where asynchronous business events add value, not as a default replacement for a simple synchronous call.
Event-driven architecture design: How wo: Assume at-least-once delivery, give events stable IDs, make consumers idempotent, acknowledge only after durable processing, and use an outbox/inbox or transactional boundary to avoid database/message dual writes. Add bounded retries, dead-letter handling, replay controls, schema versioning, ordering keys where needed, and end-to-end tracing.
Event-driven architecture incident: A po: Pause or throttle the affected consumer, route the event to a dead-letter queue after a bounded retry count, protect downstream dependencies with backoff/circuit breaking, and inspect the payload/schema safely. Fix or quarantine the event, replay deliberately, add validation and observability, and ensure one bad message cannot block an entire partition indefinitely.
Jira workflow design: How would you mode: Use separate but linked issue types with minimal required fields, clear states, owners, SLAs, and automation. Incidents capture impact and timeline, problems/RCA track systemic causes, changes capture risk/evidence, and engineering tasks deliver fixes; avoid duplicating the same information and measure flow rather than field completion.
Jira automation: How would you integrate: Have pipelines attach commit, artifact, environment, approval, test, and deployment results to the relevant change/release issue through a service identity. Monitoring can create or link incidents with deduplication and correlation IDs; synchronize status automatically but keep human decision points for risk and closure.
Jira reporting: Which metrics are useful: Useful metrics include incident count/severity, MTTA/MTTR, recurrence, change failure rate, lead/cycle time, aging, SLA breaches, and action-item completion. Raw ticket counts or story points can reward fragmentation and do not prove reliability or productivity; combine Jira flow data with SLO, deployment, and operational telemetry.
Multi-cloud architecture: When is using: It is justified by regulatory/data-residency needs, acquisitions, specialized provider capabilities, contractual risk, or a business requirement whose value exceeds added complexity. Avoid multi-cloud solely to claim provider independence: identity, networking, security, observability, skills, data consistency, and duplicated platform operations can outweigh the benefit.
Multi-cloud architecture design: How wou: Use redundant VPN or provider/interconnect partner connectivity, non-overlapping IPAM, controlled route exchange through a hub/transit design, private DNS strategy, and least-privilege firewall policy. Federate identity with short-lived credentials, centralize observability and policy where practical, encrypt traffic, and test asymmetric routing and provider failure.
Multi-cloud architecture operations: How: Define common control objectives and golden patterns in versioned Terraform modules/policy-as-code, while allowing provider-specific implementation. Centralize asset inventory, identity governance, logging, vulnerability findings, tagging, cost ownership, and compliance evidence; run scheduled drift checks and assign owners rather than forcing an unrealistic lowest-common-denominator platform.
REST APIs and microservices: How would y: Bound services around cohesive business capabilities and data ownership, not technical layers. Define resource-oriented APIs with OpenAPI, explicit schemas, validation, pagination, idempotency, errors, authentication/authorization, and compatibility rules; avoid chatty boundaries and shared databases that create a distributed monolith.
REST APIs and microservices reliability:: Use deadlines/timeouts, bounded retries with jitter only for safe operations, idempotency keys, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limits, health/readiness checks, and graceful degradation. Add correlation IDs, metrics, logs, traces, SLOs, and contract tests; retries without budgets can amplify an outage.
REST APIs and microservices security: Ho: Use OAuth/OIDC for user/service identity, validate JWT signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and scopes, and enforce resource-level authorization inside the owning service or gateway plus service. Use mTLS or workload identity for east-west calls, rotate secrets, rate-limit abuse, validate inputs, and log security decisions without sensitive tokens.
FastAPI, Spring Boot and Node.js: How wo: Choose from team expertise, ecosystem, performance profile, type/safety needs, startup/memory constraints, and operational standards. FastAPI fits Python async/data/ML services, Spring Boot provides mature Java enterprise integrations and strong conventions, and Node.js fits I/O-heavy services and JavaScript/TypeScript teams; prototype and benchmark the real workload.
FastAPI, Spring Boot and Node.js observa: Use OpenTelemetry instrumentation and a common semantic convention for service, environment, route, status, and deployment attributes. Emit structured logs with trace IDs, RED metrics, distributed traces, health/readiness endpoints, and consistent correlation/error handling through shared templates or libraries, while limiting high-cardinality labels.
FastAPI, Spring Boot and Node.js deploym: Every service needs a non-root immutable image, explicit requests/limits, readiness/liveness/startup probes, graceful SIGTERM handling, timeouts, configuration/secrets injection, autoscaling policy, disruption budget, NetworkPolicy, security context, and rollout/smoke validation. Framework-specific tuning differs, but the production contract should be consistent.
